items.title: George Benson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Red Holloway, he always got on me.

ctx.x: He was a nuisance to me, because he stayed on my back all the time about my playing not being up to par, and we fought over women all the time, because he was used to having them all. I said, “But you can’t take them all home with you Joe every night.” So if he saw me with a girl, he would say, “That’s mine you got with you.” I said, “Your what? Get out of here.” [Benson imitates a woman’s voice (indecipherable).] One time – he started – he would come by my room, bang on my door in the middle of the night, boom…

nothing, and Red would be scuffling through that. So he said, “I don’t know how you do it.” He said, “You’re going to be a monster guitar player.” He said, “Don’t pay no attention to what them cats is talking about.” We had an exciting two-and-a-half years. It was contentious.

items.title: Red Holloway interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995
items.q: him and George Benson and Joe Dukes had been playing together for oh a couple of years. And I had joined him

ctx.x: And they do the rhythm section first, they do the solo tracks after that, and all this intricate mixing.

That is so ridiculous. That is just really stupid. And I don’t care who hears it that’s stupid. That’s just a waste of time and money. The way we used to do, and the way I still do myself, is what I’ll do is like when I was working with Brother Jack McDuff, even John Mayall, now he’s a British, father of the British blues, I worked with him. We would rehearse the stuff at his house, all the changes that had to be made, then we would play it on some jobs. We’d play it maybe for a month. And I still do that, and…
